etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Ancient Greek τραγικός (tragikós, “of or relating to tragedy”), from τράγος (trágos, “male goat”), a reference to the goat-satyrs of the theatrical plays of the Dorians.

quote.citation: 2012 March-April, Jan Sapp, “Race Finished”, in American Scientist‎[1], volume 100, number 2, page 164:
quote.text: Few concepts are as emotionally charged as that of race. The word conjures up a mixture of associations—culture, ethnicity, genetics, subjugation, exclusion and persecution. But is the tragic history of efforts to define groups of people by race really a matter of the misuse of science, the abuse of a valid biological concept?

definitions.definition: Relating to tragedy in a literary work.
(in tabloid newspapers) Having been the victim of a tragedy.
(informal, chiefly predicative) Cringeworthy; tryhard; unhip; embarrassing; hopeless; indicative of (or having) a chronic lack of self-awareness.
(Australia, colloquial) An obsessive fan, a superfan

quote.citation: 2011 March 31, James Macsmith, “General Russell Crowe and his Rabbitoh minions”, in Travel, CNN:
quote.text: Within the club itself, Crowe is regarded not only as a benefactor but as a fanatic -- a Rabbitohs tragic.

quote.citation: 2013 March 13. Ricky Stuart, quoted in "Doping scandal is overwhelming league: Stuart":
quote.text: I'm a fan of rugby league. I'm a tragic of rugby league.

quote.citation: 2013 August 28, Kent Steedman, “The Knowledge: Rifled In”, in The Guardian:
quote.text: Damian was/is a football tragic, the rest of us just like it to varying degrees.
